Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic errors in the forecasts compared to true outcomes.

Looking at the examples, they all appear to be centered around EUA (EU Allowance) prices around the 60-70 EUR/ton range, with dates from February to October 2024.

Let me examine the patterns:

## Example 1 (2024-10-02)
- History shows prices drifting lower from ~67 down to ~63.6 over 18 days
- Model forecasts are generally lower than true outcomes
- The model seems to be under-predicting when prices are bottoming out

Looking at the first 10 days of Example 1:
Model: [62.93, 63.24, 62.84, 62.56, 60.95, 62.46, 65.30, 64.83, 66.22, 65.63]
True: [62.60, 62.76, 62.05, 61.76, 60.29, 62.01, 65.00, 64.62, 65.97, 65.09]

The model is consistently forecasting about 0.3-0.5 EUR higher than true prices in the bottoming section, but then catches up and under-predicts in the middle section. Looking more carefully:

Actually let me look at the pattern more systematically. The model forecasts appear to be:
1. Too low in the beginning (days 1-5): model is ~0.3-0.6 too high... wait that's backwards from what I said
2. Let me re-examine: at day 1, model says 62.93 vs true 62.60 (model 0.33 too high)
3. At day 5, model says 60.95 vs true 60.29 (model 0.66 too high)


4. At day 7, model says 65.30 vs true 65.00 (model 0.30 too high)

I notice a consistent pattern of model forecasts being slightly above true prices during initial low points. The deviations appear smallest around days 1, 7, and 9, with variations ranging from 0.3 to 0.7 currency units. This suggests a nuanced relationship between the model's predictions and actual prices, particularly in the early stages of the 30-day observation period.
